pitchHistory.title: You Are Not the Same Person Who Started Reading This Sentence
pitchHistory.summary: Personal identity is the assumption hiding beneath almost every moral and legal institution we've built — contracts, punishment, promises, self-improvement — and yet the more carefully you examine what makes you *you* across time, the less solid the ground becomes. This post interrogates the tension between the philosophical fragility of personal identity and the practical necessity of treating it as settled, asking what it would actually mean to take our best theories of the self seriously — and why we mostly can't afford to.

pitchHistory.title: The Agnosticism We Can't Afford to Ignore: What AI Consciousness Does to Our Entire Moral Framework
pitchHistory.summary: We've spent decades debating whether AI can think — but philosophers are now raising a harder, stranger question: what if we can never know whether it feels? This post examines why the unresolvability of AI consciousness isn't a technical footnote but a genuine crisis for moral philosophy, forcing us to confront how we assign rights, responsibility, and moral status when the evidence will always be ambiguous. It's a question that makes the familiar categories of ethics strange again — and that discomfort is exactly where serious thinking has to begin.

pitchHistory.title: Why Two People Can Do the Exact Same Wrong Thing — and One of Them Deserves More Blame
pitchHistory.summary: Two drivers get behind the wheel drunk. One makes it home. One kills a pedestrian. They made identical choices — yet we judge them very differently. This post digs into the philosophy of moral luck: the deeply uncomfortable idea that how much blame we deserve is partly determined by chance, not character. It's a tension that cuts across criminal justice, everyday moral intuitions, and the question of whether fairness is even coherent — and it's one that most people have never interrogated.

pitchHistory.title: The Injustice of Living Forever: Why Immortality Might Be the Most Unequal Thing We've Ever Built
pitchHistory.summary: Silicon Valley is spending billions to defeat death — and framing it as the ultimate humanitarian project. But if radical life extension arrives, it will almost certainly arrive for the rich first, and that's not just an inconvenience: it may represent the most catastrophic concentration of power in human history. This post interrogates what happens to justice, meaning, and democratic society when the wealthiest people don't just have more money — they have more time itself.
